title: A Wonder in the Sky
summary: A cloud of compassion spreads unbroken and splits the duality of being and nonbeing; in the refrain a wonder rises in the middle of the sky and Bhusuku tells himself to look at the true nature of the innate; the magic show breaks, the purity of the sense objects is understood in joy as the moon lights up the sky, and the yogi Bhusuku dispels the darkness. Munidatta reads the cloud as the purified enjoyment body of the lord of yogis spreading forth by the guru's grace (cp.30.m2), the wonder as coupled union arising in clear light (cp.30.m3), and the darkness as that of the afflictions, dispelled by the rising of the fourth joy (cp.30.m6).

flags.note: The printed heading names only the rāga. The poet's name is supplied from the attribution bhusukupādānām ('of Bhusukupāda') written before the song, which the input moves out of line 1a, and from the Tibetan heading (b+hu su ku'i zhabs kyi'o). Drop it if headings should render only the printed words.

phariā is a participle in -iā ('spread, having spread'). Taken here as the main verb, as the Tibetan line takes it ('phro, 'spreads, radiates'). It could instead be an absolutive that, with daliyā in 1b, hangs on the refrain: 'the cloud of compassion having spread..., a wonder has risen'. nirantara is 'without interval': unbroken in time, or dense, without gaps; 'unbroken' keeps both.

lines.gloss: being-and-nonbeing · duality (?) · splitting (having split) · refrain cue

flags.note: dvandala is uncertain in form and sense. The glossary's 'duality' assumes Sanskrit dvandva, 'pair, pair of opposites', with an Old Bengali suffix -la. Another division is dva(n)-dala, 'the two halves' (dala, 'half, piece'), which would make a play on daliyā, 'splitting', from the same root dal-. Munidatta does not repeat the word; his paraphrase sets 'the conceptualization of the grasped and the rest' beside being and nonbeing where it stands (cp.30.m2). Kept 'duality' per the glossary; the line's general sense (the pair being/nonbeing is split) does not depend on the choice.

The Tibetan line, dngos po dngos med rtog cing rtog cing sel, 'examining and examining, it clears away things and non-things', has no clear equivalent of dvandala: its rtog ('examine', also 'conceive') stands roughly where dvandala does, and sel, 'clear away', answers daliyā, 'splitting'.

lines.en: A [wonder]{adbhuta} has risen in the middle of the [sky]{gagana}.

flags.note: Munidatta cites the refrain as uie (উইএ), not uittā (cp.30.m3); both look like forms of 'risen' (Sanskrit udita), so the sense is unaffected. The Tibetan line has 'a great wonder (ya mtshan che ba) dawned at the centre (mthil) of the sky'.

lines.gloss: look-O · Bhusuku · innate · true-nature · refrain cue
lines.en: Look, [Bhusuku]{p-bhusuku}, at the [true nature]{svarupa} of the [innate]{sahaja}.

flags.note: pekhare is taken as the imperative pekha, 'look, see' (Sanskrit prekṣ-), with the vocative particle re; the Tibetan has ltos shig, 'look!'. sahaja saruā may be 'the true nature of the innate' or 'the innate true nature'; Munidatta has 'the true nature of innate joy' (cp.30.m3), the Tibetan lhan skyes rang bzhin.

lines.en: When it is heard, the [magic show]{indrajala} breaks apart;

flags.note: indiāla: rendered 'magic show' per the glossary (Sanskrit indrajāla), as the Tibetan line reads it (mig 'phrul). Munidatta glosses it as 'the host of the senses' (indriyasamūha), as if from indriya, 'sense' (perhaps indriya-jāla, 'net of the senses'), which breaks and flees on beholding innate joy (cp.30.m4); the Tibetan comment joins the two (mig 'phrul ni dbang po'i tshogs). The glossary bars 'senses' from the line, so his reading goes to the notes.

sunante is taken as a present participle of sun-, 'hear', in the locative ('on hearing'); jāsu, 'of which' or 'of whom', is taken to point back to the true nature of the innate (2b), rendered 'it'. Munidatta has pratīkṣaṇe, 'on beholding' (cp.30.m4), and the Tibetan comment so sor blta bas, 'by looking at'. The Tibetan line has instead gang gi yid la, 'in whose mind (the magic show was cut off)', making jāsu a person and dropping the hearing.

lines.translit: nihure ṇia mana ṇa de ulāsa || dhru ||
lines.gloss: in-stillness (?) · own · mind · not · gives · delight · refrain cue
lines.en: in stillness, one's own [mind]{citta} gives no [delight]{ullasa}.

flags.note: The Bengali has a negative: ṇa de ulāsa, 'does not give delight'. Munidatta's paraphrase has none: one's own mind, bodhicitta, by the vajra guru's grace 'gives the delight of the innate' (sahajollāsaṃ dadāti) (cp.30.m4). Nor has the Tibetan line: rang gi yid la dga' ba ster bar byed, 'gives joy to one's own mind'. Translated as printed, with the negative, because the Bengali is the reading text and the line can stand as it is (the magic show broken, the mind gives no more delight). But two witnesses against it suggest ṇa may be a copying slip, perhaps an echo of ṇia just before. Without it: 'in stillness, one's own mind gives delight.'

ṇia mana, 'one's own mind', is taken as the subject, as Munidatta takes it (nijamanaḥ, nominative, cp.30.m4). The Tibetan line makes it the recipient (rang gi yid la, 'to one's own mind'), with the one 'in whose mind' the show broke (3a) as the giver. Old Bengali leaves the case unmarked, so 'gives no delight to one's own mind' is also possible.

nihure is uncertain. Munidatta cites it as nihae and renders nibhṛtena, 'in stillness, quietly', adding 'in a form free of concepts' (cp.30.m4); 'in stillness' follows him. The -re might instead be the vocative particle seen in pekhare (2b). The Tibetan line has no equivalent, and the Tibetan comment's 'byung bas does not obviously render nibhṛta.

lines.en: Through the [purity]{visuddhi} of the [sense objects]{visaya} I understood, in [joy]{ananda},

flags.note: ānande is taken as a locative, 'in joy', as Munidatta takes it ('in the joy of cessation', cp.30.m5). The Tibetan line makes joy the object: bdag gi dga' ba rtogs, 'I realized (my) joy'. bujhjhia, 'understood', is a past participle with the agent mai, 'by me'; what was understood is not stated.

lines.gloss: of-the-sky · as · lit-up · by-the-moon · refrain cue

flags.note: The Tibetan line, nam mkha'i mthil du ji ltar zla ba shar, has the moon rise (shar) 'at the centre of the sky', in the words of the refrain (2a), where the Bengali has it light up (ujoli) the sky; Munidatta's paraphrase agrees with the Bengali (candreṇa gaganam udyotitam, cp.30.m5). ujoli may be a past form, 'lit up', or a noun, 'brightness' (compare Sanskrit ujjvala, 'bright').

lines.en: Through these [three worlds]{trailokya} it spreads so far;

flags.note: What spreads is not said; the English adds 'it' because English needs a subject. It may anticipate the darkness of 5b, with which biṣārā rhymes ('so widespread is the darkness'), or look back to the moonlight of 4b. biṣārā is taken as 'spread' (Sanskrit vistāra; or perhaps bikhāra, 'scattered', compare Hindi bikharnā, if ṣ is read as kh). The Tibetan line has 'there the three realms are spread out' (der ni khams gsum po ni rnam par brkyang). Munidatta cites the opening as eteloe and does not gloss biṣārā (cp.30.m6).

lines.gloss: yogi · Bhusuku · dispels · darkness · refrain cue

flags.note: The Tibetan line reads differently: gang shar bhu su ku yi mun pa sel, 'what has risen dispels Bhusuku's darkness'. It has no word for 'yogi' and makes Bhusuku the one whose darkness is dispelled, not its dispeller. Munidatta keeps Bhusuku as the agent but adds 'by whose rising' (yasyodayena), and quotes Saraha's 'homage to that by whose rising' (cp.30.m6), whose Tibetan (gang shar de la phyag 'tshal lo) has the same gang shar as the Tibetan line.
hebbhai is an uncertain verb form; 'dispels' follows Munidatta's spheṭayati (cp.30.m6) and the Tibetan sel, 'clears away'.

notes.text: Rāga: a melodic mode of Indian music. Each song is headed by the rāga to which it is sung; this one is Mallārī, which the Tibetan heading transcribes mal la re instead of translating it. Later Indian music knows a rāga Mallār (Malhār) of the rainy season; whether it is the same melody is uncertain.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) names the poet Bhusuku (b+hu su ku) in its heading and in the song (2b, 5b), but in Munidatta's comment calls him 'du shes gsum pa'i zhabs, 'he of the three notions' (cp.30.m1, cp.30.m3, cp.30.m6). The Sanskrit comment has Bhusukupāda throughout.

Munidatta introduces the song as Bhusukupāda setting out 'that same meaning' out of the delight of the joy of great bliss (cp.30.m1); the Tibetan has 'the meaning of reality' (de kho na nyid kyi don). Leaving out the refrain, he counts couplet 3 as his second verse, couplet 4 as his third and couplet 5 as his fourth. The refrain, the second verse and the fourth each set out 'its power' (prabhāva); the third states the praise of the path (cp.30.m3, cp.30.m4, cp.30.m5, cp.30.m6).

A cloud of compassion that spreads without a break. Mahāyāna writing sometimes likens compassion to a rain cloud that waters all alike; the song says only that the cloud spreads, and that the duality of being and nonbeing is split.

Munidatta's gloss on the couplet opens with karuṇa, 'compassion', and does not name the cloud: once being and nonbeing, the conceptualization of the grasped and the rest, have been split and made without intrinsic nature, the purified enjoyment body of the lord of yogis spreads forth (prasphurita) by the guru's grace (cp.30.m2). His 'spreads forth' answers the song's phariā; the Tibetan comment agrees (longs spyod rdzogs pa'i sku ... 'phro ba).

dvandala: a word of uncertain form. 'Duality' takes it as Sanskrit dvandva, 'pair of opposites'; it might also be 'the two halves' (dala, 'half'), in a play on daliyā, 'splitting', from the same root. Munidatta's paraphrase does not repeat it, setting 'the conceptualization of the grasped and the rest' beside being and nonbeing instead (cp.30.m2). The Tibetan line has 'examining and examining, it clears away things and non-things' (dngos po dngos med rtog cing rtog cing sel), with no clear equivalent.

Munidatta says that with the refrain the poet sets out 'its power': in clear light (prabhāsvara), the arising of the fruit, wondrous coupled union, has come about. His paraphrase thus puts clear light where the song has the middle of the sky. He then has Bhusukupāda address himself: 'O Bhusukupāda, through the guru's lineage, in the third joy, see, know, the true nature of innate joy' (cp.30.m3). The Tibetan comment agrees ('od gsal ya mtshan che ba zung 'jug gi 'bras bu shar ba).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads the line ya mtshan che ba nam mkha'i mthil du shar, 'a great wonder dawned at the centre of the sky', adding 'great'. Munidatta cites the refrain as uie rather than uittā, apparently another spelling of 'risen' (cp.30.m3).

indiāla: a magic show or conjuring display (Sanskrit indrajāla, 'Indra's net'), a stock image for what seems real and is not; the Tibetan line has mig 'phrul, 'magic show'. Munidatta takes the word as 'the host of the senses' (indriyasamūha), which breaks apart and flees on beholding innate joy, and supports this with Saraha's line on where the senses dissolve (india jathu vilīa gau) (cp.30.m4). The Tibetan comment joins the two: 'the magic show is the host of the senses' (mig 'phrul ni dbang po'i tshogs).

jāsu sunante, 'on hearing which': Munidatta has 'on beholding which innate joy' (yasya sahajānandasya pratīkṣaṇe), the Tibetan comment 'by looking at' (so sor blta bas) (cp.30.m4). The Tibetan line reads gang gi yid la mig 'phrul chad gyur pa, 'he in whose mind the magic show is cut off', and goes on, 'gives joy to his own mind' (3b).

The Bengali reads ṇa de ulāsa, 'gives no delight'. Munidatta's paraphrase has no negative: in stillness, in a form free of concepts, one's own mind, bodhicitta, gives the delight of the innate (sahajollāsa) by the vajra guru's grace (cp.30.m4). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has none either: rang gi yid la dga' ba ster bar byed, 'gives joy to one's own mind'. The translation keeps the negative of the reading text; it may be a copyist's slip.
nihure: Munidatta cites the word as nihae and renders it nibhṛtena, 'in stillness, quietly' (cp.30.m4), the sense followed here. The Tibetan line has no equivalent.

Munidatta calls couplet 3 his second verse and says it shows the power of innate joy: on beholding it the host of the senses breaks apart and flees, and one's own mind, which he calls bodhicitta, gives the delight of the innate by the vajra guru's grace. He supports each half with a line of Saraha, the second beginning 'give up thought and non-thought' (cintācinta parihara) (cp.30.m4).

Munidatta calls couplet 4 the praise of the path and makes the simile its frame: as the sky is lit up by the moon, so by me through the purity of the sense objects. 'In joy' he explains as having understood supreme joy in the joy of cessation; by that moon of innate joy the darkness of delusion was destroyed (cp.30.m5). The song itself names no darkness until 5b. The Tibetan comment agrees (gti mug gi mun pa).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads the couplet: 'the objects are pure; I realized joy (yul ni rnam dag bdag gi dga' ba rtogs), just as the moon rose at the centre of the sky (nam mkha'i mthil du ji ltar zla ba shar)'. It makes joy what is realized, and has the moon rise rather than light up the sky, in the words of the refrain (2a).

biṣārā: taken as 'spread' (Sanskrit vistāra; or perhaps bikhāra, 'scattered', if ṣ is read as kh). Munidatta cites the opening as eteloe and paraphrases: in this threefold world there is no means other than the fourth joy (cp.30.m6); he does not gloss biṣārā. The Tibetan line has 'there the three realms are spread out' (der ni khams gsum po ni rnam par brkyang).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads gang shar bhu su ku yi mun pa sel, 'what has risen dispels Bhusuku's darkness': it has no 'yogi', and Bhusuku is the one whose darkness is dispelled. Munidatta keeps Bhusuku as the dispeller but adds 'by whose rising' (yasyodayena), then quotes Saraha, 'homage to that by whose rising' (cp.30.m6); the Tibetan of that quotation, gang shar de la phyag 'tshal lo, has the same words, gang shar, as the Tibetan line.

Munidatta says the last couplet states its power because the fruit has been attained: in this threefold world there is no means other than the fourth joy, by whose rising the siddha master Bhusukupāda dispels the darkness of the afflictions (cp.30.m6). The Tibetan comment has 'apart from the four joys' (dga' ba bzhi) where the Sanskrit has the fourth joy, and agrees on the darkness of the afflictions (nyon mongs pa'i mun pa).

termsOmitted.reason: Hit in the Tibetan line only (dga' ba). The Bengali word there is ulāsa (Sanskrit ullāsa, 'delight'), not ānanda, so it is rendered 'delight' and marked with the proposed entry ullasa instead of 'joy'.

proposals.definition: Delight or elation (Sanskrit ullāsa, 'brightening, rising up'; Old Bengali ulāsa): a surge of joy. In song 30 (3b) one's own mind 'does not give' ulāsa; Munidatta's paraphrase has the mind give the delight of the innate (sahajollāsa) (cp.30.m4), and the Tibetan line has joy (dga' ba) given to one's own mind.
proposals.rationale: The word carries the crux of 30.3b and Munidatta builds a compound on it (sahajollāsa). An entry keeps 'delight' distinct from 'joy' (ānanda), the technical word for the four joys, so that the Tibetan dga' ba in this line is not mistaken for ānanda.

questions: 3b: I kept the printed negative ('in stillness, one's own mind gives no delight') and flagged it high. Munidatta (cp.30.m4) and the Tibetan line both have the mind give delight. Should ṇa be treated as a copying slip and dropped ('gives delight'), or kept with the divergence in a note?

3b: is ṇia mana the giver, as Munidatta takes it, or the receiver, as the Tibetan line has it ('gives joy to one's own mind')? And is 'in stillness' acceptable for nihure, following Munidatta's nibhṛtena?
3a: I followed the glossary's 'magic show' for indiāla (the Tibetan line's mig 'phrul), with Munidatta's 'host of the senses' (cp.30.m4) only in the notes. Confirm?
1b: keep the glossary's 'duality' for dvandala, prefer 'the two halves' (dva-dala, playing on daliyā, 'splitting'), or keep the source form until the word is settled?

5a: the English adds 'it' for whatever spreads through the three worlds, leaving open whether it is the darkness of 5b (with which biṣārā rhymes) or the moonlight of 4b. Should the line commit to one?
Heading: I added the poet's name (Bhusukupāda) from the attribution written before the song and from the Tibetan heading, although the printed heading names only the rāga. Is that the house style?
4a: ānande taken as 'in joy' (Munidatta) rather than as the thing understood, 'I understood joy' (the Tibetan line). Agreed?
